stem: An adult client with diabetic ketoacidosis has a serum potassium level of 3.0 mmol/L before insulin is started. Which action regarding potassium and insulin is expected?

options.A: Start insulin immediately and postpone potassium replacement until the glucose level falls below 250 mg/dL.
options.B: Give a potassium-wasting diuretic before insulin to reduce total-body potassium.
options.C: Withhold potassium replacement while starting insulin because insulin will correct the potassium deficit.
options.D: Begin potassium replacement and delay insulin until the serum potassium rises above 3.5 mmol/L.

rationale: The 2024 international consensus report on adult hyperglycemic crises states that when admission potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L, potassium replacement should begin and insulin therapy should be delayed until the potassium level rises above 3.5 mmol/L. Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can worsen hypokalemia, increasing the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness. Therefore D is correct. A and C would expose the client to worsening hypokalemia, while B would further deplete potassium and is not part of DKA potassium management.
educational_objective: In adult DKA with serum potassium below 3.5 mmol/L, replace potassium first and delay insulin until potassium rises above 3.5 mmol/L to avoid worsening hypokalemia and its cardiac/neuromuscular complications.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association (ADA), European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD), Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care (JBDS), American Association of Clinical Endocrinology (AACE), and Diabetes Technology Society (DTS)
source_document_title: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
source_version_date: Published June 22, 2024; Diabetes Care 47(8):1257-1275; currentness live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Section 4 > Potassium: low-normal or low potassium (<3.5 mmol/L) at admission requires potassium replacement; insulin therapy should be delayed until potassium increases to >3.5 mmol/L to avoid life-threatening arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness.
source_claim_supported: In adult DKA with potassium below 3.5 mmol/L, potassium replacement precedes insulin and insulin is delayed until potassium exceeds 3.5 mmol/L because insulin can worsen hypokalemia.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p.46: manage acute/life-threatening conditions, recognize complications and intervene, and manage fluid/electrolyte imbalance. Medical Emergencies and Pathophysiology content, printed pp.48-49.

source_original.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis has a serum potassium level of 3.0 mmol/L before insulin is started. Which sequence is expected?

options.A: Start insulin immediately without potassium replacement because potassium will rise once hyperglycemia improves.
options.B: Give a potassium-wasting diuretic before insulin because reducing total body potassium improves DKA treatment.
options.C: Withhold fluids, potassium, and insulin until glucose falls below 250 mg/dL without treatment.
options.D: Begin potassium replacement and delay insulin until the potassium level rises above 3.5 mmol/L.

source_original.rationale: Current consensus guidance recommends potassium replacement when admission potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L and delaying insulin until potassium rises above 3.5 mmol/L. Option D is correct because insulin would shift potassium intracellularly and can worsen severe hypokalemia. A, B, and C increase risk or delay needed therapy.
source_original.source_detail: Potassium management in DKA: if potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L, begin potassium replacement and delay insulin until potassium rises above 3.5 mmol/L because insulin can worsen hypokalemia and precipitate arrhythmia/respiratory muscle weakness. 2024 international consensus report, Diabetes Care 47(8):1257-1275; remains current and live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the DKA hypokalemia construct and key D, but narrowed the stem to potassium/insulin sequencing so the item does not imply that IV fluid resuscitation should be delayed. Replaced the unsupported 'withhold fluids' distractor and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a direct consensus threshold/action rule.

audit_findings.source_authority: International multidisciplinary adult hyperglycemic-crises consensus report; official NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: Consensus report published 2024 and live-rechecked 2026-08-16 with no newer conflicting adult DKA potassium threshold identified
audit_findings.exact_locator: Consensus report Section 4 > Potassium; NCSBN Physiological Adaptation/Medical Emergencies
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses the exact <3.5 mmol/L and >3.5 mmol/L thresholds from the consensus report and limits the decision to potassium/insulin sequencing. No unsupported fluid delay, glucose threshold, or diuretic strategy is included as a valid action.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because insulin should be delayed at K 3.0 mmol/L and potassium replacement should not wait for glucose <250 mg/dL.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because a potassium-wasting diuretic would worsen total-body potassium depletion.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because insulin does not correct total-body potassium deficit and can further lower serum potassium.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D follows the consensus sequence for potassium <3.5 mmol/L; the stem explicitly isolates potassium/insulin management so fluid resuscitation is outside the choice set.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address potassium/insulin management; the correct answer is not distinguished by unrelated supportive-care detail.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — electrolyte imbalance and emergency DKA management.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the consensus report potassium section, threshold direction, all options, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity and cueing. D remained uniquely correct.
